articles.title: A blind Memphis man spent 40 years collecting discarded shoes, carpet scraps and garden hoses to make strange figures for his vegetable garden; decades later, his unusual creations became part of four major US museum collections
articles.summary: In a residential backyard in Memphis, Tennessee, an unusual collection of figures gradually took shape.
articles.body: In a residential backyard in Memphis, Tennessee, an unusual collection of figures gradually took shape. Made from objects picked up from streets, alleyways and rubbish piles, the constructions were intended to serve a practical purpose: keeping birds and other pests away from vegetables. Their creator, Hawkins Bolden, returned to the task year after year, adding new figures to his garden and working with materials that most people would have thrown away. He did not set out to build an art collection or establish himself as an artist. Yet, decades after he began making them, his distinctive creations have found their way into some of the United States’ major museum collections.How a family vegetable garden sparked Bolden’s scarecrow creationsBolden's interest in making scarecrows began with his vegetable garden. He grew crops including okra, tomatoes, hot peppers and collard greens in the backyard of his family home. The produce helped feed his extended family, and maintaining the garden remained an important part of his daily life.The idea of putting up scarecrows came from a younger member of his family, who suggested that the figures could stop birds and other animals from damaging the crops. Bolden took the suggestion further than simply placing a few conventional scarecrows around the vegetable beds. He began assembling figures from whatever discarded materials he could find in the neighbourhood.Over time, the number of constructions increased. Before each growing season, he would add another set to the garden. Eventually, the figures became so numerous that they outnumbered the plants they were supposed to protect. What started as a way to safeguard vegetables developed into a long-running practice of collecting, assembling and arranging objects.Discarded everyday objects transformed into distinctive scarecrow figuresBolden worked with a wide assortment of materials, including discarded footwear, carpet pieces, garden hoses and other objects recovered from nearby streets and alleyways. Rather than following a fixed design, he combined these items into figures with faces and body-like forms.Many of his constructions had mask-like features. Holes served as eyes, while pieces of hose, shoe soles and strips of carpet became tongues, ears and other facial details. He used tools such as razors and saws to cut and shape the materials, giving each assembly its own arrangement of textures and shapes.Although the objects were made from unrelated pieces of rubbish, the finished figures shared a recognisable visual character. Their appearance varied, but the use of found materials and exaggerated facial features gave the collection a consistent identity.Bolden's work was also closely tied to the place where it was made. The materials came from the streets around his home, while the finished constructions were installed in the same backyard where he grew food. His practice continued for roughly four decades, with the garden serving as both the setting and the reason for making them.How a childhood accident left Bolden blind by the age of eightHawkins Bolden was born in 1914 in Bailey's Bottom, a neighbourhood in Memphis, Tennessee. He was an identical twin, and his brother was Monroe Bolden. The relationship between the two remained an important part of his life, and he often spoke about the bond they shared. When the boys were young, an accident occurred while they were playing baseball in a vacant lot. The incident involved his brother and resulted in Hawkins losing his sight. He became completely blind by the age of eight.This part of his life is frequently discussed alongside his later work, given the unusual circumstances in which he developed and maintained his practice. He continued making his constructions using materials that he collected and assembled, despite having lost his vision during childhood.However, his blindness is not the only context in which his work can be understood. The figures have also been recognised for their distinctive forms, repeated visual elements and use of everyday discarded objects. Their identity as a body of work rests on more than the personal circumstances of their maker.Four decades of making figures without calling himself an artistBolden did not describe himself as an artist. His constructions were made to serve a particular purpose in his garden, rather than as part of a formal artistic project. He was not working towards exhibitions or attempting to follow established ideas about sculpture. His output nevertheless developed into a substantial collection of figurative objects. The repeated use of particular materials, the attention given to facial details and the variety of forms distinguished the scarecrows from ordinary garden decorations.The objects also attracted attention beyond the neighbourhood where they were originally made. What had been assembled from unwanted household and street materials became part of a wider discussion about self-taught artists and the different ways in which creative work can emerge outside conventional art institutions.Bolden died in 2005, aged 91. By then, he had spent around 40 years making the figures that had gradually transformed his backyard into an unusual display of found-object constructions.How his backyard scarecrows gained recognition in the American art worldRecognition of Bolden's work continued after his death. His creations have entered the collections of several prominent American institutions, including the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the High Museum of Art, the de Young Museum and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Their presence in these collections marks a considerable shift in how the objects are encountered. Originally made for a private family garden in Memphis, they are now preserved and presented within established museum settings.In May and June 2024, his work was also featured in an exhibition titled Totems at Shrine, an art gallery at 368 Broadway in New York City. The exhibition ran from May 17 to June 29, 2024, bringing a selection of his constructions to a gallery audience.The exhibition presented the figures as works with a recognisable visual language, rather than simply as functional objects made to keep birds away from vegetables. Their unusual combination of salvaged materials, sculptural forms and repeated facial motifs has helped establish Bolden's place among artists whose work developed outside formal training and traditional art-making environments.For decades, the figures had stood in the backyard for a straightforward reason. Their subsequent preservation in museums has given them a different setting, but their origins remain rooted in the Memphis garden where Bolden began making them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Centre turns up heat on Zakir Naik: States, UTs get sweeping powers under UAPA to act against banned IRF
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Centre has expanded its crackdown on Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), empowering state governments and Union Territory
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Centre has expanded its crackdown on Zakir Naik's Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), empowering state governments and Union Territory administrations to freeze funds and restrict access to properties linked to the organisation. The move comes days after the home ministry extended a five-year ban on the IRFAccording to a notification issued on Thursday, the Centre has delegated these powers to states and UTs under Section 42 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA)."The Central Government hereby directs that all powers exercisable by it under sections 7 and 8 of the UAPA shall also be exercised by the state governments and the Union territory administrations in relation to the above said unlawful association,” the notification said.The notification also refers to the Centre's November 13 declaration of the IRF as an unlawful association under the UAPA. "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-sections (1) and (3) of section 3 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (37 of 1967), the Central Government has declared the Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), as an unlawful association vide notification number, S.O. 6182(E), dated the 13th November"Section 7 of the UAPA empowers the government to prohibit the use of funds belonging to an association declared unlawful. It allows authorities to issue a written order barring anyone holding money, securities or credits being used, or intended to be used, for the association from paying, transferring or otherwise dealing with them without the government's written permission.A government-appointed gazetted officer can also be authorised to inspect the person's premises, examine records and investigate financial transactions suspected to be linked to the unlawful association.Section 8, meanwhile, empowers the government to notify any place, including a house, building or part of it, a tent or a vessel, that it believes is being used for the purposes of an unlawful association.Following such a notification, the district magistrate can prepare an inventory of movable property at the premises and prohibit the use of articles suspected to be connected with the association. The magistrate can also restrict entry into the notified premises by people who were not residents there when the notification was issued. Police officers of at least the rank of sub-inspector can search people entering or found at the premises.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Man shifts from Hyderabad to Kurnool, Bharat Gas agency cancels his LPG connection instead of transferring it; consumer court orders restoration and awards Rs 20,000 in relief
articles.summary: NEW DELHIA: A district consumer commission in Andhra Pradesh has directed a Bharat Gas distributor to restore and transfer a man's existing LPG connection
articles.body: NEW DELHIA: A district consumer commission in Andhra Pradesh has directed a Bharat Gas distributor to restore and transfer a man's existing LPG connection after it allegedly cancelled the connection instead of processing his request following a change of residence. The commission also awarded Rs 15,000 as compensation for mental agony and inconvenience and Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses, holding the distributor liable for deficiency in service.Why was the man’s LPG connection cancelled?The complainant, Shaik Abdulla, a resident of Kurnool, had a domestic LPG connection with Avinash Bharat Gas Agency in Medchal-Malkajgiri, Hyderabad. After shifting his residence to Kurnool, he approached the distributor seeking transfer of his existing connection.Also read: RTO delays fancy number plate allotment, man wins Rs 2.53 lakh in reliefThe agency collected Rs 300 towards service charges. However, instead of transferring the connection, it allegedly cancelled it without informing him and issued a termination form instead of a transfer form.When Abdulla contacted the agency through WhatsApp to confirm the matter, he was advised to obtain a new gas connection. He approached the commission seeking Rs 1 lakh as compensation for mental agony and inconvenience and Rs 20,000 towards legal expenses.The distributor did not appear before the commission despite receiving notice and was proceeded against ex parte.What did the commission say?The bench comprising president Karanam Kishore Kumar and member N Narayana Reddy observed that the distributor failed to properly process the transfer request or explain why the existing connection was terminated.The commission noted that a distributor is expected to guide consumers and follow the prescribed procedure when they seek transfer of an existing LPG connection after changing residence."The opposite party cannot simply terminate the existing connection without adequately communicating the consequences to the consumer and providing appropriate assistance," the commission observed.It also noted that obtaining a fresh gas connection had become difficult amid a shortage of domestic LPG cylinders and restrictions on new connections.Final orderAnnounced on November 5, 2026, the commission partly allowed the complaint and directed the distributor to:Restore the complainant's existing LPG connection and facilitate its transfer from Hyderabad to an authorised Bharat Gas distributor in Kurnool, subject to applicable charges and regulatory requirements.Pay Rs 15,000 as compensation for mental agony and inconvenience.Pay Rs 5,000 towards litigation expenses.The distributor must comply with the directions within 45 days of receiving the order.

articles.summary: GUMLA: Four members of a family, including two brothers, were arrested in Jharkhand's Gumla district for allegedly killing two women, transporting their
articles.body: GUMLA: Four members of a family, including two brothers, were arrested in Jharkhand's Gumla district for allegedly killing two women, transporting their bodies in an ambulance and burying them in neighbouring Simdega district, police said on Wednesday.The deceased, identified as Mini Priya (28) and Radhika Kumari (20), were married to brothers Shivshankar Sahu and Navin Sahu, respectively. Police said the brothers were allegedly angered by a long-standing dispute between the two women, who had recently reconciled.The arrested accused were identified as Shivshankar, Navin, their father Sameshwar Sahu and mother Tileshwari Devi. The family hails from Samsera village under Gumla Sadar police station limits, where the murders allegedly took place.According to police, the women were allegedly killed with an axe following domestic disputes on Monday. The brothers, one of whom works as an ambulance driver, then transported the bodies in an ambulance and buried them in a deserted area in Simdega district.Their bodies were later recovered from a ditch near a dhaba in Arani Nekdarn village in Simdega and sent to Sadar Hospital in Gumla for postmortem examination. Police also recovered an axe allegedly used in the killings based on the accused's confession.The case came to light after police received a complaint from Hema Devi of Nagfeni Raputoli village under Sisai police station limits. The accused had initially approached police claiming that the two women had gone missing without informing them. However, their statements raised suspicion during questioning.Gumla SP Harish Bin Zaman said the accused confessed to the crime during sustained interrogation. He added that further investigation was underway to establish the circumstances behind the murders, including the role of other family members.The accused have been booked under sections 103(1), 238 and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Five-foot black dragon water monitor lizard ‘Phantom’ from California smashed through a shed roof, vanished for three days, then walked home safe
articles.summary: Escaped black dragon water monitor found safe in San Clemente, Orange County, after three days on the run in Southern California.
articles.body: Escaped black dragon water monitor found safe in San Clemente, Orange County, after three days on the run in Southern California. Phantom, a five-year-old lizard measuring five feet, broke through part of the roof of his backyard shed on Monday, 16 November 2026 and disappeared while cold, wet weather moved in. He walked back to the shed by himself on Thursday, 19 November, without a scratch. Rescuer Kayla Seal, who runs the nonprofit Reptile Saviour, had placed him with his foster family about a year earlier. In California, these lizards are legal to keep, provided no local rule bans them.Phantom the black dragon water monitor breaks through a San Clemente shed roof and disappearsPhantom was loose somewhere in Orange County for the whole time he was missing, and nobody knows exactly where he went. He had a decent setup, with the run of his foster family's backyard. He put his strength to use on the shed and scampered off, leaving the family worried about him.Foster mother finds the missing lizard trying to get back into his shed after three nights outsideSeal wrote that the foster mother, a reptile foster care provider in San Clemente, found Phantom trying to get back into the shed, and that he had come to no harm. KTLA in Los Angeles, which had covered his disappearance the evening before, reported that he had made his own way home.What is a black dragon water monitor? An Indonesian giant with a genetic quirk that turns it blackA black dragon is a water monitor, a big lizard native to Indonesia, with a genetic change that turns the whole animal black. Most water monitors are dark on top and pale yellow underneath, so a black dragon looks like the opposite of an albino. Only the Komodo dragon grows bigger, and the two look alike. Adult water monitors usually weigh 35 to 44 pounds, and the largest reach around 110 pounds. They have sharp claws, strong jaws, sharp teeth and a powerful tail, and they climb trees to get away from danger.Lizards cannot make enough body heat of their own, so like other reptiles, they must take warmth from their surroundings, whether from a sunny spot or a heat lamp. Phantom's shed had a heat lamp in it. A reptile that gets too cold slows down and turns sluggish, and in snakes, digestion can slow so much that food spoils in the stomach. That is why the change in the weather worried his foster family. In the wild, black dragons live near water and dig burrows, whereas Phantom's shelter was a shed with a lamp.Rescuer Kayla Seal says giant lizards like Phantom should never have been taken into captivitySeal told KTLA's Hailey Winslow that she personally does not believe animals like Phantom should have been brought into captivity in the first place, because they are so large and need so much socialisation and "so much space". By 20 November, she was working through many inquiries from people hoping to give him a permanent home, many of them prompted by the attention his escape received. She wrote that the rescue was looking for a proper forever home for him, and until one turned up, he was back in the shed he had broken out of.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Wyoming Supreme Court provides green light to a proposed wind energy project; neighbouring landowner challenged this development over potential property value losses and concerns about state land leasing rules
articles.summary: Wyoming's Supreme Court has cleared a major hurdle for the proposed Pronghorn H2 wind energy project, allowing it to move forward despite a legal
articles.body: Wyoming's Supreme Court has cleared a major hurdle for the proposed Pronghorn H2 wind energy project, allowing it to move forward despite a legal challenge from a neighbouring landowner. The dispute centres on a proposed development near Glenrock that would place hundreds of wind turbines across state and private land. While the landowner argued that the project could affect property values, the surrounding landscape and other interests, the court upheld the state's decision to lease public land for the development, bringing an end to a lengthy legal and political dispute.Why the Wyoming Supreme Court allowed the Pronghorn H2 wind project to advanceThe Wyoming Supreme Court ruled on November 3, 2026, that the State Board of Land Commissioners had acted within its authority when it approved a lease for the Pronghorn H2 wind energy project. According to Wyoming Public Media, the unanimous decision reversed an earlier district court ruling that had invalidated the lease.The project, planned near Glenrock in Converse County, is designed to supply electricity to a hydrogen production facility. Its approval had faced opposition from neighbouring landowner Michael Stephens and Stephens Land and Livestock, who challenged the state's decision to lease the land.The Supreme Court determined that the state land board had followed its rules when approving the agreement. It also rejected arguments that the board had failed to secure the greatest possible financial benefit from the land or properly considered other interests connected with the development.However, the ruling did not mean that the wind farm could immediately begin construction. The project must still undergo a separate permitting process before the Industrial Siting Council.Why the neighbouring landowner challenged the wind farmThe legal challenge was brought by Michael Stephens, whose property borders the proposed development area. As reported by Cowboy State Daily, Stephens argued that the project was being approved without the state following its own leasing rules.He also raised concerns about the potential impact on wildlife, the value generated from state-owned land and the future use of mineral resources beneath the project area.Stephens has a personal connection to the surrounding landscape. Speaking to Cowboy State Daily during the earlier stages of the dispute, he described the area as beautiful and compared its natural surroundings to Wyoming's Teton and Bighorn mountain regions. His family's connection to the property dates back to 1912, when his ancestors first homesteaded there.The Supreme Court recognised that Stephens had the legal right to challenge the lease because of his proximity to the proposed wind farm. Wyoming Public Media reported that the justices considered the potential effects on views and property values substantial, immediate and financial in nature.However, recognising his right to bring the case did not mean the court agreed with his arguments against the lease. The justices ultimately decided that the state board had acted within its authority.The wind project became a political dispute in WyomingThe controversy extended beyond the courtroom and created disagreements among Wyoming's senior elected officials.According to Cowboy State Daily, the State Board of Land Commissioners approved the Pronghorn H2 lease in April 2025. The board comprises 5 elected officials. Governor Mark Gordon, Auditor Kristi Racines, Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder and Treasurer Curt Meier supported the approval, while Secretary of State Chuck Gray opposed it.Gray questioned the decision, and the disagreement continued for months. The dispute became particularly heated during a January 8, 2026, meeting in Douglas, when Gordon challenged Gray during a tense exchange.The disagreement intensified after a district court judge struck down the lease in December 2025. Judge F Scott Peasley decided that the state's wind energy leasing rules required a project to connect to the electricity transmission grid.Since Pronghorn H2 was primarily intended to supply power to a hydrogen plant rather than necessarily feed electricity into the wider grid, the district court found that the lease did not meet the relevant requirements.Wyoming Attorney General Keith Kautz appealed the decision, arguing that the lower court had interpreted the wording of the rules too narrowly. The Supreme Court eventually agreed with the state's position.What did the Supreme Court say about the state's land leasing rulesA central issue in the case was how Wyoming's rules define wind energy projects eligible for state land leases.The district court had interpreted the rules as requiring wind farms to generate electricity for the transmission grid. However, the Supreme Court disagreed with that reading and decided that the wording did not prevent a wind energy project from supplying electricity to a hydrogen production facility.Cowboy State Daily reported that the justices unanimously upheld the board's authority to approve the lease. The court also rejected concerns that the development would prevent future mineral leasing. Companies would still be allowed to lease mineral resources beneath the state-owned land, provided their activities did not interfere with the wind farm.This distinction was important because the ruling did not give the wind project unrestricted control over every resource beneath the leased land.Future of the Pronghorn H2 wind energy projectWyoming Public Media reported that the project must obtain approval from the Industrial Siting Council, a process that could take several years. This stage could also provide an opportunity for concerns raised by neighbouring landowners to receive further consideration.The plaintiffs also have the option to request a rehearing within 15 days of the ruling, although such requests are rarely granted.The project is part of a broader development planned across a substantial area of Wyoming. Cowboy State Daily reported that Pronghorn H2 is scheduled to cover approximately 46,000 acres in total, including 13,838 acres of state-owned land.Wyoming already has a significant wind energy industry. According to figures cited by Wyoming Public Media, the state has approximately 1,500 operating wind turbines with a combined generating capacity of around 3,700 megawatts, equivalent to about 25% of its total electricity generation capacity.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi government on Friday opened former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal's controversial 'Sheesh Mahal' residence on Flagstaff Road to the media, showcasing its interiors and furnishings, which the BJP has alleged were purchased using public money at exorbitant prices.The government plans to open the bungalow to the public through a ticketing system in the coming days.During the media tour, officials displayed expensive furnishings, including a chandelier worth Rs 11.56 lakh, a sofa priced at Rs 5.47 lakh, chairs costing Rs 5.58 lakh, a central table worth Rs 6.79 lakh and curtains valued at Rs 5.69 lakh. The government is expected to introduce an online booking system this week.The bungalow, under the PWD's maintenance, has eight bedrooms, 12 toilets, a jacuzzi bath, spa, expensive carpets, five OLED TVs, and other amenities.Delhi minister Kapil Mishra said the opening would allow people across the country to see the property and alleged that public funds had been misused during Kejriwal's tenure."Starting today, the public in Delhi and across the country will be able to see this 'Sheesh Mahal'. It has been opened to the media today, and through your cameras, the entire nation will witness the sordid game of corruption and plunder that Kejriwal played," Mishra said.He alleged that the furnishings and materials had been sourced from different countries, citing marble imported from Vietnam and crockery and tables procured from abroad. Mishra also accused the former chief minister of spending lavishly on the residence while Delhi was struggling during the Covid-19 pandemic.Officials said the entry ticket is likely to cost around Rs 20, while senior citizens and college students may be allowed free entry.The government is also considering hiring a private hospitality company to manage the property, which is proposed to host official conferences, lunches and meetings."The public viewing will be for a limited period of time. After that, the plan to hand it over to a private hospitality company is in the works. It will be finalised soon," a senior government official said.Located at 6, Flagstaff Road, the bungalow served as Kejriwal's official residence during his tenure as Delhi chief minister from 2015 to 2024. The BJP coined the term 'Sheesh Mahal' during its campaign for the February 2025 Assembly elections, alleging that public money had been spent excessively on its renovation.After Kejriwal and his family vacated the bungalow, the PWD conducted an extensive audit of its interiors. articles.title: Five years after former farmland on England's Isle of Wight was left to recover, wildlife monitors report bird numbers almost tripling, butterfly counts rising 117% and bumblebee abundance increasing 64%
articles.summary: Nature has a remarkable way of finding its way back to spaces we think it might have forgotten.
articles.body: Nature has a remarkable way of finding its way back to spaces we think it might have forgotten. Every time we think we are the saviours of nature, it shows us who really holds the reins. We saw this during the time of COVID, when chirping birds, jumping frogs and tiny sparkles of light, the fireflies, came crawling back into the streets, leaving everyone in awe of the situation. Mountains became visible, and rivers and oceans began to recover within a mere two years, which is insignificant in the larger timeline of nature.Not on the grand scale of that situation, but an English farmland is having a sort of renaissance of its own too. On England's Isle of Wight, five years of rewilding have now offered a glimpse of just how much nature can recover when human intervention gives way to more natural processes.According to a new report released by the Hampshire & Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust, wildlife numbers have increased significantly across two former intensively farmed sites on the Isle of Wight. The findings show that bird numbers at Wilder Little Duxmore have almost tripled, while butterfly counts at Wilder Nunwell have increased by 117% and bumblebee abundance by 64%. The two sites have been undergoing rewilding since 2020 and 2022, respectively.How wildlife has returned to the former farmland on the Isle of WightThe recovery has been documented at two sites, Wilder Little Duxmore and Wilder Nunwell, where the Hampshire & Isle of Wight Wildlife Trust has been allowing nature to reclaim land previously used for intensive agriculture. Rather than continuing conventional farming practices, the project focuses on restoring natural habitats and allowing wildlife to return with minimal human interference.At Wilder Little Duxmore, bird numbers have almost tripled over the five-year monitoring period. The site has also recorded the arrival of 20 bird species that were not previously observed there. Meanwhile, Wilder Nunwell has seen a 117% rise in butterfly counts and a 64% increase in bumblebee abundance. Nine new butterfly species have also been recorded at the site.These changes are particularly encouraging because birds, butterflies and bumblebees depend on healthy habitats to feed, breed and survive. Their return shows how the restoration work is helping create more suitable conditions for wildlife, rather than simply changing the look of the farmland.What changed when the farmland was left to rewildMore than simply leaving the land untouched, rewilding involves giving natural processes the opportunity to restore habitats that may have been affected by years of intensive human activity. At the two Isle of Wight sites, the Trust has been working to improve the conditions in which wildlife can thrive, allowing vegetation to grow, habitats to develop and different species to return.The benefits have also extended beyond the increase in wildlife numbers. The Trust's report points to improvements in soil and water quality, both of which are important for maintaining healthy ecosystems. Better soil conditions support plant growth, while healthier water systems help sustain the insects, birds and other animals that depend on them. These changes may take years to become fully visible, but they show why restoring a landscape requires looking beyond the number of species recorded in a survey.What makes the findings particularly encouraging is that the recovery has been observed over a relatively short period. Five years may seem like a long time when measured against our everyday lives, but for an ecosystem, it is only the beginning of a much longer process.An important lesson from the Isle of Wight is that nature does not always need grand interventions to begin recovering. Sometimes, it simply needs us to step back and give it space to grow. Land that once served a very different purpose is now supporting more birds, butterflies and bees, reminding us that the damage caused by years of human activity does not necessarily have to be permanent. Five years is only a small part of an ecosystem's life, but the changes recorded so far offer a hopeful glimpse of what can happen when we allow the natural world to find its balance again.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jagan Mohan Reddy's YSRCP to back NDA's Delimitation Bill push in Parliament but with a rider
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Jagan Mohan Reddy-led YSRCP will support the NDA government's push for the Delimitation Bill in Parliament, provided it ensures regional
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Jagan Mohan Reddy-led YSRCP will support the NDA government's push for the Delimitation Bill in Parliament, provided it ensures regional balance, party sources told news agency ANI on Friday.The support from the YSRCP will strengthen the NDA's numbers as the Centre prepares to bring the legislation back to Parliament during a special sitting.Party sources told ANI that the YSRCP would support the Bill if it is introduced with provisions "ensuring regional balance."The development assumes significance as the government seeks to secure the two-thirds majority required to pass the legislation, which failed to clear the floor test during the Budget Session.Apart from the YSRCP, Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) has also adopted a softer stance on the proposed legislation. Party leader Supriya Sule recently indicated that there might be "something good" about the Bill, adding that the party would not "blindly" oppose it simply because it was in the opposition.The Union government's latest move to reconvene Parliament has added to the political focus on the proposed legislation. Ending the suspense, the government on Thursday moved to convene a short session of Parliament from November 30, during which it is expected to bring back the delimitation Bills to implement the women's reservation law from 2029.The proposed exercise is expected to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 from 550, with the government seeking to ensure that the expansion addresses concerns over regional representation.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju announced on Thursday that the government had requested Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla to reconvene the Lower House on November 30 and Rajya Sabha chairman C P Radhakrishnan to call a sitting of the Upper House on December 2 to transact "essential government business".Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) chief Mayawati on Friday launched a sharp attack on the Samajwadi Party (SP) over its recently released 'Manifesto of the People's Will' for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, dismissing it as "little more than empty rhetoric" and a "money-minded manifesto" rather than a genuine commitment to public welfare.In a post on X, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister said the SP's manifesto was similar to its 'PDA' (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) initiative and reflected the saying "all show, no substance".Mayawati alleged that the SP had consistently followed a "narrow-minded, casteist and pro-big business" approach that went against the interests, welfare, dignity and security of poor people, Dalits, backward classes, Muslims and other sections of society.She also cited the SP's alleged preference for a wealthy businessperson over supporting the PDA in the recent biennial Rajya Sabha elections from Uttar Pradesh as an example of its political approach.Questioning whether such policies could address the state's problems, including poverty, unemployment, backwardness and migration, Mayawati said the SP's manifesto was more concerned with financial interests than public welfare. She further alleged that the party would continue to field wealthy candidates and strongmen rather than people committed to public and social interests.Defending her party's record, Mayawati said the principles of "work for every hand" and "the rule of law through the law" belonged to the BSP and had been implemented during all four of its governments in Uttar Pradesh.She also accused the SP of having a record of opposing reservations for Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs) and Other Backward Classes (OBCs), and of contributing to caste-based hostility and riots in the state.In her post, she described the SP's promises and declarations as "electoral deception and trickery", urging voters to remain cautious.Mayawati pitches BSP as authentic Ambedkarite partyWith Assembly elections approaching in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Punjab, Mayawati called for strengthening the BSP, describing it as the only authentic Ambedkarite party capable of translating the ideals of the Constitution into reality.“Given that the general assembly elections—particularly in Uttar Pradesh, as well as in Uttarakhand and Punjab—are fast approaching, it is imperative to effectively translate the noble intent of Babasaheb Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar’s Constitution into reality. This cannot be achieved through the mindset or working culture of narrow-minded, feudal, or casteist parties; rather, it can only be realised through the advancement of the BSP—the sole, authentic Ambedkarite party—which guarantees the welfare of all sections of society and ensures the safety of their lives, property, and religious beliefs, while fostering the upliftment of the 'Bahujan Samaj’," she said.Mayawati said the BSP aimed to establish the rule of law in Uttar Pradesh and promote a governance model centred on public welfare, social well-being and development.“So that an 'iron rule of law' can be established here in UP, along with a governance model rooted in the principle of 'the welfare and happiness of all '—prioritising public interest, social well-being, and development. This would enable all sections of society—currently plagued by poverty, unemployment, backwardness, and the distress of forced migration—to lead a prosperous life filled with peace and happiness,” she added.The BSP, which governed Uttar Pradesh from 2007 to 2012, was reduced to a single seat in the 2022 Assembly elections despite securing more than 13 per cent of the vote share.The party failed to win a single seat in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.SP-Congress seat-sharing talks continueMeanwhile, the SP is preparing to contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections in alliance with the Congress. The two INDIA bloc partners are continuing negotiations over seat-sharing, with the SP having offered 26 seats to the Congress in the initial round of discussions.The Congress, however, has sought 120 seats and is unwilling to accept a lower number, according to sources.The SP is seeking to return to power after consecutive defeats in the 2017 and 2022 Assembly elections. It won 111 seats in the 2022 polls.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'If you offer zero seats, result will be zero': Congress MP Imran Masood's message to SP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Imran Masood on Friday renewed his criticism of INDIA bloc ally Samajwadi Party over seat-sharing for the poll-bound Uttar Pradesh.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Imran Masood on Friday renewed his criticism of INDIA bloc ally Samajwadi Party over seat-sharing for the poll-bound Uttar Pradesh. He questioned the Akhilesh-led party's reluctance to offer the grand old party more seats.Taking a swipe at SP, Saharanpur MP Masood said the Samajwadi Party's tally of 37 Lok Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh was made possible in part by Rahul Gandhi's contribution to the INDIA bloc's campaign."It was because of Rahul Gandhi that you (Samajwadi Party)managed to win 37 seats (2024 Lok Sabha Elections). We aren’t saying you didn’t contribute; we are saying that we, too, secured victories. We showed a big heart—but must it always be us who shows a big heart, every single time? Can’t you show a bit more generosity?" he told news agency ANI.The Congress MP also questioned the SP's approach to seat-sharing, saying the party should contest the seats itself if it was unwilling to give them to Congress."If you offer zero seats, the result will naturally be zero. Why don’t you contest these seats yourselves? You go ahead and win them—after all, you claim to have a formula for winnability." he added.Masood's latest remarks came a day after Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge publicly advised him to "talk less and work more", amid concerns that his repeated criticism of the SP could strain ties between the INDIA bloc allies.Addressing party workers at a Constitution Day programme in Lucknow on Thursday, Kharge acknowledged Masood's enthusiasm and his commitment to raising the party's concerns but underlined the importance of collective efforts.“Imran Masood ji bade josh ke saath apni baat rakhte hain. Main roz unhe TV par sunta hoon. Kabhi-kabhi thoda zyada josh mein bhi baat karte hain. Lekin humein baaton se zyada kaam karna hai. Isliye hum jitna milkar kaam karenge, utna hi aage badhenge (Imran Masood ji puts forward his views with great enthusiasm. I hear him regularly on television, where he speaks quite forcefully. But more than statements, we have to work on the ground),” Kharge said.The Congress chief also acknowledged Masood's commitment and his consistent efforts to fight for the party in Parliament.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Arrest me': CJP's Abhijit Dipke dares Mumbai Police, defies lookout circular at Nagpur rally
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder and national convener Abhijeet Dipke on Thursday addressed a protest rally in Nagpur, challenging Mumbai
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder and national convener Abhijeet Dipke on Thursday addressed a protest rally in Nagpur, challenging Mumbai Police to arrest him. The rally came even as Mumbai Police issued a Look Out Circular (LOC) against him in connection with an FIR linked to the party’s October 2 protest in Mumbai."There is a lookout notice against me by the Mumbai Police. There is police bandobast here and they are looking for me. Where is Abhijeet Dipke? I am here in Samvidhan Chowk. What will you do? Arrest me,” Dipke said, according to news agency ANI.“I have been in jail twice. Don't show me the fear of jail," he added, while addressing the CJP's 'Save Democracy, Save Constitution' rally at Samvidhan Chowk on Constitution Day.Mumbai Police issued LOCs against Dipke and CJP co-convenors Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das on Thursday. The circulars are linked to an FIR registered at Shivaji Park police station on October 3 over the party's protest held the previous day.The FIR names the organisers and between 400 and 500 unidentified attendees, invoking Sections 189 and 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), relating to unlawful assembly and disobedience to an order promulgated by a public servant.At the Nagpur rally, Dipke accused the BJP-led Centre of undermining the Constitution and alleged that institutions across the country had been hijacked."The government is acting against the Constitution. Not a single institution is left that has not been hijacked," he said.He also warned against what he described as the government's use of intimidation. "You have destroyed the country by intimidating people but this will not be tolerated. Show as much fear as you want for two more years. 2029 is approaching. This is India after Jantar Mantar," Dipke said.CJP co-convenor Ranka said the party would expand its activities beyond protests in major cities. "We will go to every village, interact with people and give a voice to the youth," he said.The LOCs come amid a separate legal challenge by Das, who was stopped from boarding a flight to the United Kingdom at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport on November 23. He was scheduled to attend a panel discussion at Oxford.During proceedings before the Delhi High Court on Thursday, the Centre told Justice Amit Mahajan that the travel restriction had been initiated at the request of Maharashtra Police. Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma cited discrepancies in Das's educational background, address and parentage during record checks.Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, appearing for Das, argued that his client had not received prior notice or the underlying LOC order. "He has a valid passport and has a valid visa. He cannot be stopped from travelling as it is his fundamental right," Sibal told the court, according to ANI.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolly Parton grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 siblings; decades later, her $500 pledge to students helped bring their high school dropout rate from 35% to 6%
articles.summary: Long before Dolly Parton became a household name, the hills of East Tennessee were home.
articles.body: Long before Dolly Parton became a household name, the hills of East Tennessee were home. Her childhood in the Smoky Mountains, spent in a large family with limited resources, remained a recurring presence in her music and later charitable work. Even after moving to Nashville to pursue a career, she maintained close ties with the region where she grew up. Her connection to Sevier County eventually extended well beyond music and tourism. In 1988, Parton established the Dollywood Foundation. Two years later, it launched the Buddy Program to address high school dropout rates in Sevier County.Dolly Parton's early life in the mountains of TennesseeParton grew up as one of 12 children in a small two-room cabin in rural Tennessee. The family had neither electricity nor running water, and money was often limited. Her early surroundings later found their way into her songs, many of which drew on the landscape, traditions and everyday lives of people in Appalachia.She left the mountains after completing high school and moved to Nashville, where her music career began to take shape. Yet her departure did not mean leaving her hometown behind. Parton continued to return to East Tennessee, maintaining a connection with the communities that had shaped her childhood.That attachment eventually became part of her business and philanthropic decisions. Rather than limiting her involvement to occasional visits or public appearances, she invested in projects intended to create opportunities for people living in the area.How Dolly Parton turned Dollywood into a Tennessee tourism landmarkA major turning point came in 1986, when Parton became a co-owner of an amusement park in Pigeon Forge and helped transform it into Dollywood. The attraction gave visitors another reason to travel to the Smoky Mountains, a region that had already drawn tourists to Great Smoky Mountains National Park and nearby Gatlinburg. The park grew into one of Tennessee's leading tourist destinations. Its expansion brought employment opportunities and supported businesses across the surrounding communities. According to Associated Press, Dollywood generates approximately $1.8 billion annually and is the largest employer in Sevier County.For a region that had relied heavily on its natural attractions and established tourism centres, the development marked a significant change. Local businesses benefited from the additional visitors, while the park itself became an important source of jobs. Parton's involvement also gave the attraction a recognisable identity. She regularly appeared at seasonal openings and other events, keeping her association with the business visible to visitors.The education initiative that changed lives in Sevier CountyHer contribution to the county was not limited to tourism. In 1988, Parton established the Dollywood Foundation, with an initial focus on addressing the high number of students leaving school before graduation in Sevier County. According to the Dollywood Foundation, the Buddy Program was introduced in 1990, when participating classes had a dropout rate of approximately 35%. The initiative paired seventh- and eighth-grade students and promised each participant $500 upon graduating from high school. The scheme was designed to give young people an additional reason to remain committed to their education, while the buddy arrangement provided a form of peer support along the way.According to Fortune, David Wear, a former mayor of Pigeon Forge, was among those who experienced the programme during his school years. He was in eighth grade when it began and later recalled how the promise of financial assistance encouraged students to see their education through to graduation. According to figures shared by the Dollywood Foundation, Sevier County's dropout rate eventually fell to 6% after the initiative was introduced. The reduction represented a substantial change from the levels recorded when the programme began.How Dolly Parton’s book-gifting programme reached millions of childrenParton's interest in education also extended to younger children. What began as a local effort to encourage reading eventually developed into the Imagination Library, a book-gifting programme that reached families far beyond her home state. The initiative was established to help children develop an interest in books from an early age, with registered participants receiving books through the post. Its reach gradually expanded beyond the United States to include Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Australia.According to the foundation, the programme has distributed more than 325 million books since its launch. Its growth turned a community-focused project into an international literacy initiative, allowing children in different countries to access books during their early years. The programme also reflected a concern that had been present in Parton's own upbringing. She understood the limitations families could face when money was tight and educational resources were not always readily available.The $2 billion disaster that brought Parton back to her communityParton's involvement in Sevier County became particularly visible again in 2016, when wildfires swept through parts of the Great Smoky Mountains and reached nearby Gatlinburg. Fortune reported, the disaster killed 14 people and caused extensive destruction. Around 2,500 buildings were damaged or destroyed, with estimated losses reaching $2 billion. Families were displaced, homes were lost and local businesses faced the difficult task of rebuilding.Parton directed her foundation to provide financial assistance to affected residents. The support included funds for families who had lost their homes and scholarships for students whose lives had been disrupted by the fires.Wear later credited her fundraising efforts and public profile with helping the community recover. Her involvement brought attention and financial support at a time when residents were dealing with the immediate consequences of the disaster.The singer who never turned away from her Tennessee rootsParton's relationship with East Tennessee also carried significance beyond the money invested in businesses, schools and community projects. The region has often been associated with narrow stereotypes about rural Appalachian life, something she encountered throughout her career.Ted Olson, a professor of Appalachian studies at East Tennessee State University, told the Associated Press that Parton challenged those perceptions through her public presence and efforts to encourage people to visit the area. Her music frequently drew on the region's culture, while her business ventures brought visitors into communities that might otherwise have received less attention.Her career connected two very different sides of her life. She became an internationally recognised performer, but continued to direct attention and resources towards the part of Tennessee where she had grown up.You use AI every day. articles.title: Supreme Court grants bail to former AAP MLA Naresh Balyan in organised crime case
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday granted bail to former Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) MLA Naresh Balyan in an organised crime case concerning his alleged
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday granted bail to former Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) MLA Naresh Balyan in an organised crime case concerning his alleged links with gangster Kapil Sangwan.A bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Singh passed the order.Balyan was arrested on December 4, 2024, in a case registered under the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act (MCOCA). The arrest came on the same day a trial court granted him bail in a separate extortion case involving allegations of links with Sangwan.The Delhi Police Crime Branch had accused the former Uttam Nagar legislator of acting as a "facilitator" for an alleged organised crime syndicate. The prosecution cited multiple FIRs registered against members of the alleged syndicate, claiming that it had engaged in continuing unlawful activities and amassed substantial illegal wealth.In August 2026, the Delhi high court refused to grant Balyan bail in the MCOCA case, observing that 17 FIRs had been registered against the alleged syndicate, indicating continuing unlawful activity. Justice Manoj Jain held that prolonged incarceration alone could not be the decisive factor for granting bail in serious cases involving stringent provisions of the law.The high court's decision came days after a trial court discharged Balyan in the separate extortion case, holding that the prosecution had failed to establish the foundational threshold required for framing charges.Additional chief judicial magistrate Paras Dalal had observed that there was "not a single piece of evidence" to prima facie establish any prior meeting of minds between Balyan and absconding gangster Kapil Sangwan.Challenging the denial of bail in the MCOCA case, Balyan had maintained that there was "no shred of evidence" against him and described the case as "completely frivolous". He had also alleged that the proceedings were politically motivated.The Delhi Police, however, had opposed his release, arguing that the investigation was at a crucial stage and that his release could hamper the probe.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Farhat Jabeen challenges gender norms as Pakistan's first female jet ski instructor
articles.summary: Farhat Jabeen, a 35-year-old mother of four, is challenging gender barriers in Pakistan’s water sports sector as a jet ski instructor at Kallar Kahar
articles.body: Farhat Jabeen, a 35-year-old mother of four, is challenging gender barriers in Pakistan’s water sports sector as a jet ski instructor at Kallar Kahar Lake, offering women visitors an opportunity to ride with a female instructor in a sport traditionally dominated by men.Gripping the handlebars, Jabeen executes sharp turns across the lake, sending water spraying into the air. Her work has made jet ski rides more accessible to women who may be reluctant to ride with male instructors because of conservative social customs."A woman should be brave," Jabeen told news agency AFP on the shores of the lake, around 125 kilometres south of Islamabad.She has spent the past two years taking women on jet ski tours and riding alongside other instructors. However, she said entering a male-dominated workplace was initially difficult."It was very difficult when I first came here for this job. Many objections were raised about me," she told AFP."Some said 'You're a woman, how will you work among men?'" she added.With guidance from a senior instructor, Jabeen spent a month learning to operate the jet ski and follow safety procedures. She now works up to 11 hours a day, inspecting boat engines, cleaning equipment and repairing damaged life jackets before taking visitors on rides.Despite the demanding schedule, she said her family helped her overcome fatigue."When I go home and meet my children in the evening, when I see them, all my tiredness goes away," she said.Instructor Tariq Mahmood told AFP that Jabeen's appointment had made it easier to accommodate women visitors. Ever since she joined, "it has become completely easy for us to send women to ride" with her, he said.Muhammad Abbas Ashraf, manager of Kallar Kahar's Tourism Development Corporation, said women had faced difficulties accessing jet ski rides before her appointment."When we first introduced the jet skis, women who visited here faced difficulties, because we could not have them sit with us and ride," he told AFP.Qamar-un-Nisa, a 50-year-old school principal who rode with Jabeen, praised the appointment. "Appointing a female instructor is a very admirable step," she told AFP.Jabeen urged women to seek employment despite social resistance, "There is nothing to be afraid of," she said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Parliament special session: Delimitation, women's quota, SIR row - what’s on the cards
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A special sitting of Parliament will begin on November 30, with the government expected to consider reviving its push for a constitutional
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A special sitting of Parliament will begin on November 30, with the government expected to consider reviving its push for a constitutional amendment linking women’s reservation to delimitation. The move could set the stage for a fresh political confrontation with the Opposition.The Lok Sabha will reconvene on November 30 and the Rajya Sabha on December 2, with the sittings scheduled to conclude on December 3, subject to government business.The government has not officially confirmed which Bills will be taken up. However, speculation has gathered pace over the proposed Delimitation Bill and the implementation of 33 per cent reservation for women in Parliament and state legislatures ahead of the 2029 general elections.What is on the government's agenda?Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju said the government had requested Lok Sabha speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha chairman C P Radhakrishnan to reconvene the Houses to transact “essential government business”.“Subject to exigencies of the business, the sitting of both Houses may conclude on December 3, 2026,” Rijiju said in a post on X.The special sittings will be an extension of the Monsoon Session, which was adjourned sine die on August 13 and subsequently prorogued.The proposed legislation seeks to increase the Lok Sabha's strength from 543 to a maximum of 850 seats through delimitation, paving the way for 33 per cent reservation for women in legislative bodies.Why the Bill failed in AprilThe Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha during the special sitting on April 16-17. It received 298 votes in favour and 230 against, with 11 members abstaining. At the time, the House had 528 members and the Bill needed 352 votes to pass.The draft had not provided for a proportional 50 per cent increase in seats across states, a key concern for regional parties, particularly those from southern India. The government has since explored a formula to increase seats by 50 per cent in every state while retaining the existing inter-state share based on the 1971 Census.Protests against SIRThe opposition parties are also expected to carry their protests against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation into Parliament.Numbers game: DMK, NCP-SP and YSRCPThe BJP leaders are banking on support from the DMK, NCP-SP and breakaway factions of the Trinamool Congress and Shiv Sena for the delimitation bill. The DMK has 22 Lok Sabha MPs and the NCP (SP) has eight. Both parties have indicated they could consider backing the proposal if their states' share of seats is protected.NCP-SCP MP Supriya Sule on Wednesday said the proposed Delimitation Bill should first be introduced and its full text made available for scrutiny. “Let the bill be introduced first; let us have the full bill in our hands. Once we have it, we can discuss it—and perhaps it will turn out to be a good one,” she told reporters.YSRCP is also expected to support the Delimitation Bill, according to sources quoted by news agency ANI. Meanwhile, Congress and NCP (SP) are stepping up coordination ahead of the sitting, with the parties summoning their MPs to discuss the proposed legislation and the Opposition's strategy.Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh said the government was hoping to secure its “super-tainted” two-thirds majority. “A fight is on,” he said.Cabinet meeting, BJP strategyThe Union Cabinet is scheduled to meet at Sewa Teerth in New Delhi at 1 pm on Friday.The meeting comes as the BJP holds a two-day gathering of its national office-bearers and state in-charges at the PUSA campus on November 27 and 28. Discussions are expected to cover organisational strategy, upcoming Assembly elections and coordination between the Centre, states and the party organisation.The Cabinet meet is also likely to discuss the delimitation-linked women's quota, ANI wrote, quoting sources.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: How outing for young couple in Nagpur forest turned into horror: Man sexually assaults woman, thrashes boyfriend
articles.summary: NAGPUR: A 19-year-old woman was allegedly sexually assaulted in an isolated stretch of Amrai forest near Sonegaon lake in Nagpur on Monday night after a
articles.body: NAGPUR: A 19-year-old woman was allegedly sexually assaulted in an isolated stretch of Amrai forest near Sonegaon lake in Nagpur on Monday night after a man attacked her boyfriend and drove him away.The accused allegedly overpowered the woman while she was with her boyfriend at a secluded spot. He is also suspected of stalking the couple before the attack.The survivor approached Sonegaon police on Tuesday, accompanied by family members, and lodged a complaint. Police said the accused allegedly recorded videos of her, snatched her valuables and threatened to circulate the footage on social media before fleeing.Sonegaon police and the crime branch have launched an investigation. They are examining CCTV footage from entry and exit points in the area and have released two sketches of the suspect based on the survivor's description.Police examine CCTV footage, scan criminal recordsAccording to police, the couple was walking through an isolated part of the forest late Monday when the accused intercepted them. He allegedly assaulted the woman's boyfriend and chased him away before attacking the woman despite her resistance.The couple initially did not report the incident. They later discussed it with family members before approaching the police.An offence involving sexual assault and robbery has been registered. The woman's medical examination was under way when the report was filed.Investigators are also checking the records of criminals previously involved in similar offences. Police have shown the survivor photographs of suspected offenders as part of the identification process.The crime branch has been activated, and neighbouring police stations, including Pratap Nagar and Hingna, have been alerted.Residents raise concerns over isolated stretchesThe assault has renewed concerns about the safety of Amrai forest, a popular green space near Sonegaon lake frequented by morning walkers, senior citizens, women and families.Residents said they had repeatedly alerted police about the presence of suspected criminal elements in the forest. They also expressed concern over poorly lit and secluded stretches, which they said had increasingly become gathering points for people allegedly involved in illegal and inappropriate activities.Although the area attracts a considerable number of visitors during morning and evening hours, residents said some isolated portions remained vulnerable because of inadequate surveillance."Residents of Sonegaon and adjoining areas are raising safety concerns after a 19-year-old girl was sexually assaulted on Monday at Amrai, a popular green space frequented by morning walkers, senior citizens and families," said a local resident.Nirbhaya squad patrols under scrutinyThe incident has also raised questions about surveillance in the area, despite regular patrols by all-woman Nirbhaya squads formed to prevent eve-teasing and crimes against women.Residents said the presence of couples and people allegedly engaging in anti-social activities in secluded parts of the forest had been a longstanding concern."The assault has highlighted the challenges of policing isolated areas and keeping a close watch on spots that may attract anti-social elements," said a resident.Another local resident said the lack of adequate monitoring in deserted stretches could make them vulnerable to crime."We fear that such desolate spots, if left without adequate surveillance, could become vulnerable to criminal activity," said a local resident.Police are continuing their search for the unidentified suspect and examining available evidence to establish his identity.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Nagpur | Silver Rate in Nagpur | Bank Holidays in Nagpur | Public Holidays in Nagpur | Petrol Price in Nagpur | Diesel Price in Nagpur | CNG Price in Nagpur | LPG Price in NagpurStay updated with the latest Nagpur news. articles.title: Adopted son of former Kentucky governor seeks financial support in parents' divorce, alleges years of mistreatment; court rejects claim but orders nearly $66,000 in legal fees
articles.summary: The adopted son of former Kentucky governor Matt Bevin has lost his bid for financial support from his parents in their divorce proceedings, but a
articles.body: The adopted son of former Kentucky governor Matt Bevin has lost his bid for financial support from his parents in their divorce proceedings, but a Kentucky judge has ordered both of them to pay nearly $66,000 towards his legal fees. Jonah Bevin, 20, had intervened in his parents' divorce case, alleging years of neglect and mistreatment, including being sent to residential facilities as a teenager. In an order issued on November 25, Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela J. Johnson rejected his request for retroactive and future child support, finding no legal authority under Kentucky law allowing an adult child to establish such a claim independently. However, the judge found that both parents had acted in bad faith during the proceedings and ordered them to contribute towards his lawyers' fees.Why did the former Kentucky governor's adopted son seek financial support?Jonah is one of four children adopted by Matt and Glenna Bevin from Ethiopia. The couple also have five biological children. Glenna filed for divorce in May 2023, and their divorce was finalised in March 2025.Jonah intervened in the divorce proceedings in May 2025, seeking financial support from his parents. He alleged that they had abandoned him at the age of 17 at the Atlantis Leadership Academy, a residential facility in Jamaica, where he and other young people were subjected to abuse and neglect.After the facility was closed by child-welfare authorities, Jonah was placed in the custody of Jamaican child-welfare authorities. He alleged that his parents failed to help secure his return to the US and that outside advocates assisted him. However, the judge's order records that Matt Bevin eventually paid to have his son flown back to the US from Jamaica.Jonah's lawyers also questioned the validity of his high-school diploma, arguing that it had been issued by an online academy that was not accredited. The judge noted that little evidence had been presented about his diploma and educational qualifications.The case attracted wider attention amid the controversy surrounding the troubled-teen residential treatment industry. Celebrity Paris Hilton travelled to Jamaica to show support for young people removed from the Atlantis Leadership Academy.What did the judge say about the mistreatment allegations?During a hearing in July 2026, the court heard testimony from Jonah, his mother Glenna and child-welfare advocate Donna J. Post about his upbringing and experiences at residential facilities.The judge considered accounts of alleged abuse and neglect alongside testimony about Jonah's behaviour during his childhood. These included competing accounts from Jonah and his mother about the family's circumstances and his experiences at residential institutions.Glenna testified that Jonah had been difficult to manage and had sometimes displayed threatening and aggressive behaviour. She also said that Matt had largely handled family finances and made most of the decisions concerning their son's placements at residential facilities.The judge questioned the selection and quality of those institutions, observing that, based on the testimony, none appeared to be evidence-based mental-health programmes and that they had been selected through word of mouth.The court also noted that Matt had claimed Jonah possessed a high-school diploma from an accredited programme but had not provided the promised documentation to establish this.Court rejected his financial support requestJudge Angela J. Johnson ruled that Kentucky law did not provide legal authority for Jonah to independently establish a child-support claim against his parents.The judge found that the law did not allow an adult child to initiate proceedings to establish retroactive or future child support for himself. She also concluded that the evidence presented was insufficient to determine an appropriate amount of financial support, even if such a claim had been legally available.Consequently, Jonah's request for retroactive and future child support was denied.Why were Matt and Glenna ordered to pay nearly $66,000?Despite rejecting the support claim, the judge found that both parents had acted in bad faith during the discovery process, particularly over the disclosure of their financial information.According to the order, the parents had delayed providing financial documents and other information required during the proceedings. The judge found that their conduct was intended to delay and frustrate the case.The court ordered Matt to pay $47,216 towards Jonah's legal fees, while Glenna was directed to contribute $18,477.50. The combined award amounts to $65,693.50, with both payments due within 30 days of the order.The judge also noted that Jonah's lawyers had billed $66,693.50 for their work between March 2025 and September 2026, with $1,000 already paid.Can Jonah still seek his father's help with higher education?The judge also considered Jonah's request to enforce a provision in his parents' marital settlement agreement requiring Matt to fund each child's post-secondary education or equivalent training for up to four years.The court recognised Jonah as a third-party beneficiary of that provision, meaning he could potentially enforce the educational funding commitment against his father.However, the judge denied his request at this stage because Jonah had not applied to a post-secondary programme, formally requested the money from his father or demonstrated that Matt had breached the agreement.The ruling therefore leaves open the possibility of further proceedings over educational funding if Jonah meets the relevant conditions in the future.The November 25 order is described as final and appealable. While his request for child support has been rejected, the ruling leaves the education-funding provision open to potential enforcement in a subsequent proceeding.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Behind the closed doors of a house in southwest Delhi's West Sagarpur, an entire family was allegedly running a drug syndicate, with a woman,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Behind the closed doors of a house in southwest Delhi's West Sagarpur, an entire family was allegedly running a drug syndicate, with a woman, her son, daughter and another female relative suspected of being part of the network.Now, all four are facing preventive detention under the stringent Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (PITNDPS) Act while police try to dismantle the alleged family-run operation.Delhi govt's home department has forwarded detention orders against 11 people under the PITNDPS Act, 1988, according to an official communication dated Nov 23. The letter, addressed to the superintendent of Tihar Jail, directs prison authorities to take necessary action on the orders, which were accompanied by individual grounds of detention.The West Sagarpur family accounts for four of the 11 people named in the communication.According to police records, the alleged network involved two sisters, one of whom had 30 previous cases registered against her since 1996, while the other had 25 cases dating back to 1995.The latter's two children, a daughter and a son, were also allegedly involved in criminal activities, with eight cases registered against the daughter since 2016 and five against the son since 2018. The four are collectively involved in 68 cases. Police sources said the alleged drug supply source was in Firozpur, Punjab."The family was allegedly operating a syndicate, which needed to be broken. The anti-narcotics cell of South West district examined various aspects of the network, including its financial dealings, and built a strong case for invoking the PITNDPS Act," a source said.Investigators are also looking into properties allegedly acquired by the family using proceeds from drug sales. Sources said the financial trail is being examined to identify assets that may have been purchased through the alleged illegal trade.The objective, they added, is to strike at the financial foundations of the suspected network rather than merely target those allegedly involved in selling narcotics.The remaining names are spread across the capital. Two individuals each belong to Outer North and East districts, while one each is from Outer and North districts. Another person from Dwarka has also been named.The PITNDPS Act allows preventive detention to curb illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances. The stringent provision is used against people suspected of continuing such activities and is aimed at preventing them from carrying on illicit drug trafficking.Police sources said the latest action was prompted by concerns that the accused continued to engage in criminal activities, posing a challenge to law and order. The wider crackdown is aimed at disrupting suspected drug networks operating across Delhi.Earlier in Aug, a 51-year-old drug trafficker was arrested and booked under the PITNDPS Act. Dharamveer Singh, a resident of Inderpuri, became a major supplier of illegal ganja.The drug was smuggled from south India to the capital.
