articles.title: Psychology says people who feel a sudden urge to jump when standing near a height may experience the‘call of the void,’ a phenomenon researchers have examined in relation to intrusive thoughts
articles.summary: You are standing on a balcony, looking at the view below, when an unexpected thought crosses your mind: What if I jumped?
articles.body: You are standing on a balcony, looking at the view below, when an unexpected thought crosses your mind: What if I jumped? The thought may appear for just a second, leaving you startled. You have no intention of doing anything dangerous, yet you wonder why your mind produced such an alarming idea in the first place.A similar experience can occur while standing on a bridge or looking down from a tall building. Some people describe it as an unexplained urge to jump, even when they have no desire to hurt themselves.This experience is commonly known as the 'call of the void', a French expression translated as ‘L'Appel du Vide.’ Psychologists studying the phenomenon use another term: the High Place Phenomenon (HPP). Research suggests that this sudden thought does not necessarily indicate a hidden wish to die. It may instead be connected to how the brain processes danger, fear and unwanted thoughts.What is the ‘call of the void’ and why does it happen?The High Place Phenomenon refers to the sudden experience of imagining or feeling an urge to jump when standing at a height. It is often described as an intrusive thought because it appears unexpectedly and may feel completely out of character. One explanation comes from a 2012 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.Researchers studied 431 undergraduate students to understand how frequently people experienced this phenomenon and whether it was necessarily connected to suicidal thoughts. The researchers proposed that the experience could result from a misinterpreted safety signal. In other words, when someone stands near a dangerous height, the brain may quickly register the possibility of falling and trigger a warning. The person may consciously interpret this sudden awareness of danger as an urge to jump.The study found that the experience was not limited to people who had considered suicide. More than half of the participants who had never experienced suicidal thoughts reported experiencing aspects of the phenomenon at least once.The researchers also found a relationship between anxiety sensitivity and the high place phenomenon. Anxiety sensitivity refers to the tendency to fear or become particularly aware of the physical and psychological sensations associated with anxiety.Their findings suggested that the sudden thought could sometimes reflect a person's heightened awareness of danger rather than an actual desire to act on it.Why does an unwanted thought feel so disturbing?One reason these experiences can be unsettling is that they seem to contradict what a person actually wants. Someone standing on a balcony may be enjoying the view and feeling perfectly comfortable. The sudden appearance of a dangerous thought can therefore feel confusing. The person may start questioning why they imagined something they would never want to do.Psychologists describe thoughts that conflict with a person's intentions, values or sense of self as ego-dystonic. Such thoughts can appear without being consciously invited or wanted.The important difference is between having a thought and wanting to act on it. The appearance of an unwanted thought does not automatically mean that a person intends to carry it out.However, not every experience should be dismissed as harmless. Research has found associations between the high place phenomenon and suicidal ideation in some groups, even though the experience also occurs among people without a history of suicidal thoughts.What does further research say?More recently, a 2025 study published in Frontiers in Psychiatry using responses from 476 adults. Unlike earlier research that mainly examined thoughts about jumping from heights, this study explored similar unwanted impulses in different situations, including while driving or standing on a train platform.The researchers examined how frequently these thoughts occurred, how alien they felt to the individual and what people did to manage them. The findings also pointed to associations with anxiety, depression, stress and suicidal thoughts, highlighting why the experience deserves further study.When should someone take these thoughts seriously?An occasional, unwanted thought about jumping from a height is not, by itself, proof that someone is suicidal. However, it is important to pay attention to its nature and frequency.If the thoughts become persistent, cause significant distress, involve an actual desire to harm oneself or are accompanied by thoughts of suicide, professional mental health support is important. Anyone who feels at risk of acting on such thoughts should move away from the dangerous situation and seek immediate help.The research on the call of the void offers an important distinction: the mind can produce a frightening thought without that thought reflecting what a person wants. Understanding this difference can help explain why an otherwise ordinary moment at a height can sometimes trigger such an unexpected and disturbing experience.You use AI every day. articles.title: Psychology says confident children don't let fear decide their actions; what Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's fearless approach to fast bowlers teaches parents about raising self-assured kids
articles.summary: A fast bowler runs towards the crease, sends a delivery flying at the batter and expects a defensive response.
articles.body: A fast bowler runs towards the crease, sends a delivery flying at the batter and expects a defensive response. But 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi often seems to have a different plan. Instead of allowing the speed of the delivery to dictate his next move, he looks for an opportunity to attack. His fearless approach to fast bowling has made him one of the most exciting young batters in Indian cricket. But beyond the sixes, records and remarkable strokeplay, there is an interesting lesson for parents.How do children develop the confidence to face situations that appear intimidating? Why do some children attempt difficult things while others hesitate because they are afraid of making mistakes? Psychology research offers some useful answers. And while a cricket match cannot be directly compared with the challenges children face while growing up, Sooryavanshi's journey provides an interesting starting point for understanding confidence, preparation and the importance of believing in one's abilities.The lesson is not to raise children who never feel afraid. It is to help them develop the confidence to try, even when something feels difficult.Confidence grows when children get opportunities to practiseOne reason Sooryavanshi's batting stands out is that his aggressive approach was not developed overnight. According to a report by Hindustan Times, his childhood coach Manish Ojha revealed that the youngster would sometimes face 500 to 600 deliveries during a practice session. If he wanted to improve a particular shot, he would repeatedly practise that stroke.He was also exposed to older and more experienced bowlers from a young age, including Under-19, Under-23 and Ranji Trophy players. This gave him opportunities to face challenges beyond his age group and become familiar with different bowling styles.This connects with an important psychological concept called self-efficacy, which refers to a person's belief in their ability to accomplish a particular task. Psychologist Albert Bandura identified successful experiences of overcoming challenges as an important source of self-efficacy. When children attempt something difficult and gradually become better at it, they develop greater trust in their abilities.For parents, the takeaway is simple: do not always make things easier for children. Give them age-appropriate challenges and opportunities to practise. Whether it is learning to ride a bicycle, speaking in front of a class or participating in a competition, allowing children to try repeatedly can help them recognise their own progress.Let children experience challenges instead of protecting them from everythingA parent's first instinct is often to protect a child from disappointment, embarrassment or failure. However, preventing children from experiencing every uncomfortable situation can also limit their opportunities to develop confidence. A study published in the Journal of Anxiety Disorders in 2013, titled 'You can do it! The role of parental encouragement of bravery in child anxiety treatment', examined how parents encouraged children to approach situations that made them anxious.The researchers found that children whose parents encouraged brave behaviour tended to show better treatment outcomes. The study highlighted how allowing children to approach difficult situations, make mistakes and experience discomfort can help them develop confidence in their ability to cope.This does not mean parents should force children into situations that overwhelm them. Instead, they can provide reassurance while encouraging small steps towards overcoming a challenge. For instance, if a child is nervous about participating in a school competition, parents can help them practise, acknowledge their concerns and encourage them to give it a try. The goal is not to remove every fear but to help children discover that they can handle situations even when they feel nervous.Allow children to make decisions and trust their abilitiesAnother important part of developing self-confidence is giving children the freedom to make age-appropriate decisions. A 2024 study published in Behavioral Sciences, titled 'The Relationship between Parental Autonomy Support and Children's Self-Concept in China: The Role of Basic Psychological Needs', examined 3,109 children aged 6 to 13.The researchers found a significant relationship between parental autonomy support, children's psychological needs and their self-concept. The study suggested that allowing children to make choices, respecting their perspectives and supporting their interests can contribute to how they see themselves.It also found that parental control had a consistently negative relationship with children's self-concept. The researchers emphasised that children need both appropriate independence and parental involvement. This offers an interesting parenting lesson.Parents do not have to make every decision on behalf of their children. Allowing them to choose their hobbies, solve age-appropriate problems and take responsibility for small tasks can help them develop a sense of independence. For example, instead of immediately telling a child how to complete a school project, parents can ask, "How do you think we should approach this?" Such conversations allow children to think independently and understand that their opinions matter.Teach children that mistakes are part of growing upPerhaps the biggest lesson from Sooryavanshi's cricket journey is that confidence does not mean getting everything right. Even talented athletes experience poor performances, difficult matches and disappointing results. What matters is how they respond afterwards. In November 2026, before his record-breaking 204-run innings against UAE in Doha, Sooryavanshi had experienced a relatively lean period. Speaking about that phase, he admitted that he was distracted and worried about his performances.He also revealed that a conversation with his idol Yuvraj Singh helped him work through those concerns. He subsequently reviewed his batting, identified areas he needed to improve and returned to the crease with a clearer approach. This is particularly relevant to parenting. A 2025 study examining 231 recorded conversations between mothers and their eight-year-old children explored how discussions about disappointment and failure were associated with children's fear of making mistakes.The research highlighted the importance of acknowledging children's emotions, helping them develop an action plan and identifying resources they can use to deal with setbacks. Parents can put this into practice by changing how they respond when children fail. Instead of asking, "Why did you get this wrong?", they can ask, "What did you learn from this experience?" or "What would you like to try differently next time?" This helps children understand that one disappointing result does not define their abilities.Raising children who believe in themselvesVaibhav Sooryavanshi's batting offers more than an example of fearless cricket. His early exposure to challenging bowlers, repeated practice and willingness to trust his strengths illustrate how confidence can develop through experience. For parents, the lesson is not to raise children who are fearless all the time or expect them to succeed at everything they attempt.It is to create an environment where children feel supported enough to try unfamiliar things, make mistakes, ask questions and learn from difficult experiences. Sometimes, this means stepping back instead of immediately solving their problems. At other times, it means offering encouragement when they doubt themselves.Children do not become self-assured simply because adults keep telling them they are capable. They develop confidence when they get opportunities to experience their own capabilities. And perhaps that is the most valuable lesson parents can take from the young cricketer's journey: The aim is not to teach children that they will never face difficult situations but to help them believe they can find a way through them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Community Connect: Chennai's cosmic calling - A date with the stars
articles.summary: From spotting constellations with the naked eye to capturing distant galaxies through telescopes, Chennai's astronomy enthusiasts are taking their
articles.body: From spotting constellations with the naked eye to capturing distant galaxies through telescopes, Chennai's astronomy enthusiasts are taking their curiosity beyond the ordinary. Through community stargazing sessions, astrophotography and school outreach programmes, they are bringing the wonders of the universe closer to people of all ages.'We want people to experience the night sky beyond textbooks'“Our vision is to make astronomy accessible to everyone, irrespective of age, background or scientific knowledge. Through regular stargazing sessions, school outreach programmes and hands-on learning, we want people to experience the night sky beyond textbooks. We believe curiosity is the first step towards understanding the universe, and our community provides that platform,” says Siva, founder of Chennai Astronomy Community.‘What starts as stargazing can grow into a passion for science’“Astronomy is becoming an increasingly popular hobby in Chennai, especially among youngsters interested in stargazing and astrophotography. What begins as a hobby often develops into a passion for scientific observation, as people learn about star clusters, colours and different types of stars. Our community also conducts free school outreach programmes, offering practical exposure that is often missing from classrooms. Anyone can explore the night sky without spending a penny; all it takes is curiosity and a view of the sky from your terrace,” explains Manick Rajendran (60), an investor and amateur astronomer.‘Our monthly Star Parties take us closer to the universe’“I have been part of this community for nearly five years, though my interest in astronomy dates back to the 1990s, when I made telescopes using ₹10 lenses, microscope eyepieces and cardboard. The community has further developed my interest in astrophotography and celestial observation. Every month, we organise overnight Star Parties at darker locations such as Maduranthakam and Cheyyar, where members observe galaxies, nebulae and star clusters through telescopes. Even children join these sessions to learn and explore together,” says Vijay Devakumar (45), a technical writer at an IT company.‘The community bridges the gap between curiosity and practical learning’“Being part of this community has given me opportunities to learn astronomy through practical experiences, outreach programmes and stargazing sessions outside the city. I could explore the subject more deeply only in my 30s, and the community helps bridge the gap in awareness and practical learning. It also provides a safe space for women, with strict rules prohibiting alcohol and cigarettes during Star Parties,” says Jagadeeshwari (30), an IT professional.‘An astronomy passport makes every skywatching session count’“You don't need a telescope to observe the night sky; anyone can begin by spotting constellations with the naked eye. Our community welcomes people of all ages, from college students to senior citizens in their 70s and mothers bringing their children. During space-watch sessions, members observe celestial objects through telescopes and record discoveries such as M35, M81 and nebulae in an astronomy passport, helping them track their progress and deepen their knowledge,” says Sandhya Balakrishnan (38), an IT professional.‘There is room for everyone under the night sky’“I joined the community in March, and astronomy feels like an often-overlooked hobby. Every time we look through a telescope, we discover something new, which deepens our curiosity about science. The community also teaches members to handle equipment, set up telescopes, use astrophotography cameras and identify celestial objects. There is something for everyone, regardless of their experience,” explains Anupam Roy (40), a music educationist.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Imran Masood refused to temper his criticism of the Samajwadi Party over seat-sharing for the poll-bound Uttar Pradesh, despite
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress MP Imran Masood refused to temper his criticism of the Samajwadi Party over seat-sharing for the poll-bound Uttar Pradesh, despite party chief Mallikarjun Kharge's call for unity. Claiming he was being "cornered from all sides" and made a "villain", Masood questioned, "Does BJP's defeat rest only on my shoulders?", taking another swipe at the INDIA bloc ally over its approach to the proposed alliance.Speaking to news agency ANI on Friday, Masood said Kharge had acknowledged his efforts and appreciated his work, while maintaining that he would continue to raise concerns in the Congress's interest."Kharge ji has acknowledged my efforts; he is appreciating my work. I am prepared to sacrifice my very life for the progress of my party. I am being cornered from all sides, as if I am a villain."Masood added, "I am making demands for my party; I am fighting for my party. I will always speak in the interest of my party. An alliance is being formed; does the entire responsibility of ousting the BJP rest solely on my shoulders? Does it not rest on yours (SP) as well?"The party MP also questioned the SP's approach to allocating constituencies, arguing that the Congress should not be offered seats where it had little chance of winning.“Give us seats; we can contest and win. We need both quality and quantity... You take the Chief Minister’s post. There is no dispute here regarding the Chief Minister. But why are you trying to undermine your ally? Why do you want to belittle your ally? You started launching direct attacks against me; why? I hadn’t said a single word against you," he said.He further argued that the Congress's contribution to the alliance should not be measured only by its past electoral performance."The Congress is zero. You keep reminding us of our standing, but if you think so little of our standing, why do you even need us? You have the formula for winnability; you have everything, so why do you need us at all?... We are zero—but wherever we align, we multiply the impact tenfold. It was because of Rahul Gandhi that you (SP) managed to win 37 seats (2024 Lok Sabha Elections). We aren’t saying you didn’t contribute; we are saying that we, too, secured victories. We showed a big heart, but must it always be us who shows a big heart, every single time? Can’t you show a bit more generosity?" he told ANI.The disagreement intensified after the SP reportedly offered 26 seats as a starting point and announced five candidates while negotiations were underway. Masood had objected to the move, saying: "We are not beggars... Somewhere, this is very hurtful: that you will dictate terms like this."On Thursday, Kharge, addressing the Congress's Samvidhan Raksha Sammelan in Lucknow, said Masood spoke with enthusiasm but stressed the need for collective effort. "But more than statements, we have to work on the ground," he said.The Congress is reportedly seeking around 130 seats, while the SP's initial offer was 26.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Swift seizure of small islands': China's amphibious drill using civilian ships threatens Taiwan
articles.summary: China is conducting a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in its southeastern province of Fujian, testing a new method of bringing troops and heavy
articles.body: China is conducting a weeks-long amphibious landing drill in its southeastern province of Fujian, testing a new method of bringing troops and heavy equipment ashore by linking civilian vessels to form a floating bridge, according to satellite images and a research report.The exercise is taking place in Dacheng Bay, about 280 km (175 miles) from Taiwan's main island, Reuters reported.According to the agency, the drill was first detected on November 1 by geospatial data company ingeniSPACE, whose analysis showed vessels assembling and dismantling an 800-metre (2,600-foot) floating bridge between November 1 and 16.The drill involved eight civilian vessels, including four barges, two semi-submersible vessels and two powered vessels, along with four landing craft. Smaller support vessels and Chinese navy ships were also present nearby. No purpose-built bridging equipment was observed, suggesting the military was testing how existing civilian maritime resources could be used to create temporary landing infrastructure during combat."The People's Liberation Army appeared to be rehearsing low-signature methods to provide logistical support to forces that could be involved in a first island chain invasion scenario," Jason Wang, chief operating officer of ingeniSPACE, told Reuters.A senior security official briefed on the exercise confirmed its details and said the drill was designed to "practise the swift seizure of small islands". The official described it as "very targeted" at contingencies along the first island chain, stretching from Japan through Taiwan and the Philippines.The official said the exercise appeared to be part of this year's "All-Military Strategic Exercise". China's defence ministry did not respond to a request for comment. On Thursday, it described its military training in the region as "entirely legitimate and reasonable".Taiwan's defence ministry said it was aware of Chinese military activity in Dacheng Bay, including the use of civilian vessels, and was assessing its implications for security in the Taiwan Strait.China claims Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out using force to bring the island under its control.Amphibious landing drillsMilitary attaches based in Asia said China appeared to be continuously refining its coastal exercises, reflecting the challenges of attempting an amphibious landing across waters as wide as the Taiwan Strait.The exercise is being conducted near Dongshan Island, which Chinese President Xi Jinping visited in 2024.The island was also the site of a major Cold War-era victory for the People's Liberation Army in 1953, when Chinese forces repelled an attempted invasion by Republic of China troops.The latest exercise indicated that China's military was increasingly focusing on operations involving groups of islands, the senior security official said, while cautioning against overstating the drills' battlefield value."There is still some distance between innovation and fantasy," the official said, adding that barges would be "live targets" in wartime.

articles.title: Famine expect to rise due to global conflict, El Nino, warns UN
articles.summary: El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.
articles.body:
Hunger ‌is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six ⁠months, mainly due to armed conflict and extreme climate events, two United Nations agencies said in a new report.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Friday that Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen ⁠faced the gravest threats of famine , driven by violence, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather, including the El Nino phenomenon.

Listings in the report, released twice a year through the Global Network Against Food Crises, have risen from 13 hotspots in June, with ⁠Chad, Uganda and parts of both Southern Africa and Central America added, while Lebanon was removed.

Armed conflict and violence were driving hunger in 12 of the 16 hotspots, the report said, as soaring food, energy ⁠and transport costs were eroding people’s ability to feed themselves.

El Nino, which is set to intensify to exceptional levels in the coming months according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots: Southern Africa, the Central American Dry Corridor and northeastern Uganda.

Covering December 2026 to May 2027, the agencies warned that shrinking humanitarian funding was affecting efforts to avert catastrophe.

In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1bn to $2bn.

“While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote the FAO and WFP.

While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks – including risk of famine – re-emerged within a few years.”

In Sudan, famine remains a risk ⁠in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan through January 2027, as fighting disrupts food production, markets and aid deliveries.

The agencies also identified famine risks in parts of Somalia and South ‌Sudan, where escalating violence has compounded an already desperate humanitarian situation.

Afghanistan, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Gaza were also classified as areas of very great concern.

Gaza was ‌downgraded ‌from the highest level of concern after small improvements in food security following the October 2025 “ceasefire” . But agencies warned that conditions remained fragile in Gaza, while in the occupied West Bank, acute food insecurity is expected to worsen.

articles.title: Lottery winner arrested by ICE days after claiming $1 million prize
articles.summary: An East Boston man who won $1 million on a scratch ticket earlier this month has been arrested by U.S.
articles.body: An East Boston man who won $1 million on a scratch ticket earlier this month has been arrested by U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement, the agency said Wednesday morning. Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales won the $1 million prize in the Massachusetts State Lottery’s “$2,000,000 50X Cashword” scratch ticket game, the lottery announced last week in a press release that included a photo of Velasquez holding a giant check. They said he chose the cash option for the prize, receiving a one-time payment of $650,000 before taxes. He said at the time that he planned to save and invest the winnings. He purchased the winning ticket at Sumner Market in East Boston. The store gets a $10,000 bonus for its sale of the ticket. Less than a week after the lottery announced his win, ICE said in a social media post that officers had arrested Velasquez-Morales on Tuesday during operations in East Boston, saying he was in the country illegally from El Salvador. “Welcome to the ERO [Enforcement and Removal Operations] Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!” ICE Boston said in a post on X. ICE said Velasquez-Morales entered the U.S. illegally on May 15, 2013, and was ordered removed by an immigration judge on April 24, 2014. It was not immediately clear whether Velasquez-Morales had an attorney. ICE said he will remain in its custody pending his removal from the U.S.

articles.title: Canada’s top court largely upholds Quebec’s religious symbols ban
articles.summary: Quebec’s ban on teachers and police wearing religious symbols such as hijabs and turbans on the job remains in place.
articles.body:
A landmark ruling by Canada’s Supreme Court has largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law, leaving in place a ban on public school teachers, police officers and some other public employees wearing religious symbols at work.

The ruling settles a years-long legal battle over a law that has forced some workers to choose between their careers and how they practise their faith.

The court left the ban in place, but upheld an exception to a separate rule requiring elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly to uncover their faces, finding the requirement infringed upon their democratic rights.

The National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), one of the groups that challenged Bill 21, called the ruling “a dark day in our constitutional democracy”.

Speaking after the ruling, NCCM’s chief executive Stephen Brown said, “ In our country, in the 21st century, entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are.”

The court also weighed in on a question that goes beyond Quebec — how far governments can go in using the notwithstanding clause.

The clause is part of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It lets federal and provincial governments keep a law in force even if it violates certain Charter rights, including freedom of religion and the right to equality, shielding it from court challenges. The override lasts up to five years and can be renewed. Quebec used it when it passed Bill 21 in 2019 and renewed it in 2024.

On Friday, the Supreme Court found Quebec had used the clause lawfully and that it can be used before a court rules on whether a law violates Charter rights.

“It is not open to the courts to place additional limits on the exercise of the override power,” said the decision.

Four of the seven justices also agreed that judges can formally declare that a law violates those rights even if the notwithstanding clause keeps the law in effect. Such a declaration would leave the law in place, but “vindicate affected individuals” and let citizens know how their rights are being temporarily overridden by their representatives, the justices wrote.

Only three of the justices would have issued one in this case, so the court issued none.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, which also challenged Bill 21, said the ruling “sends a message that even shielded laws cannot escape scrutiny entirely”.

“But for the people this law affects every day, that door remains closed,” said the CCLA. “Bill 21 has already denied a generation of Quebecers their chosen profession in public service because of their faith. That is discrimination, and it is why we took on this case.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told the CBC after the ruling that his colleagues in Ottawa were “carefully studying” the ruling of more than 500 pages.

“What’s important is that all legislatures, very much including also Parliament, are doing their utmost to respect the rights of all Canadians, including those in the minority,” he said.

The ruling was welcomed by Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who said it was a victory for the province’s approach to secularism, which he described as distinct from the rest of Canada’s.

“We worried about social peace if such a fundamental choice were to be invalidated by the Supreme Court,” he said.

Brown of NCCM said the ruling came as governments across Canada were losing their restraint with their use of the notwithstanding clause. He pointed to Saskatchewan’s use of it in legislation affecting LGBTQ youth and Alberta’s use of it to impose a collective agreement on teachers.

“It was intended to be an instrument of last resort, and now it has become an ordinary instrument of government,” he said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose government intervened in the case to defend the use of the clause, celebrated the decision as “a win for provincial rights”. She said elected legislatures should have the final say on important questions.

“That’s true for Quebec and it’s true for every province, including Alberta,” she wrote on X.

Quebec passed Bill 21 in June 2019 , saying it would protect the religious neutrality of public institutions. It bars people in certain public jobs from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs, turbans and kippahs while at work. Teachers who were already in their posts on March 27, 2019, were able to continue wearing them as long as they stayed in the same role with the same employer.

The law has reshaped lives , leading to people losing their jobs and in some cases, leaving Quebec to continue working in their professions. Some Muslim women have decided to take off their hijabs while at work in order to keep their jobs.

Quebec has since widened the restrictions to support staff and volunteers at school under Bill 94 and to daycare staff under Bill 9. In both cases, Quebec invoked the notwithstanding clause.

Quebec’s government has said it wants to go further by barring elementary school students from wearing religious symbols.

Nevien Waly, who wears a hijab and was told she could not volunteer at her children’s school under Bill 94, said she had expected the court to uphold the law, but was holding out hope that it might go the other way.

“I didn’t think that it would be overturned, but I’m still disappointed,” she told Al Jazeera after the ruling. “I’m sad for myself, worried about the future of our kids.”

Waly said she worried the ruling would embolden people to openly mistreat those who wear religious symbols, something she said she had already experienced more often in recent years, as she started wearing the hijab and Quebec widened its restrictions.

The case was heard by seven justices. Chief Justice Richard Wagner, writing for three justices, said Bill 21 was rooted in Quebec’s “legitimate and historical commitment” to keeping the state secular. He concluded that the Quebec government had “validly used” its power to keep the law in force.

In a partial dissent, Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin wrote there was no serious question that the law violates the right to freedom of religion. They described how Muslim women had been turned away from jobs because they wear a hijab and how the law had prevented people from taking promotions or being transferred to new roles because they would lose their exemptions. They said the law “non-trivially influences life choices and mobility”.

“The Act’s effects are not experienced equally,” they wrote. “They fall most heavily on Muslim women.”

The justices acknowledged that the consequences went beyond work, noting reports of more verbal and physical abuse from some members of religious minorities. They said the law affected people’s “basic sense of belonging in Canadian and Quebec society”.

Before the ruling, Waly said she could not imagine leaving Quebec, where she grew up and where much of her family lives. On Friday, she said she was encouraging her children to excel in school so they would have the option to leave.

“I don’t see a good future in Quebec,” she said.

articles.title: 50% uniform seats increase, delimitation on 2011 census: What govt's new Bill proposes
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Days before the special parliamentary session, the government has moved to withdraw the Delimitation Bill, 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Days before the special parliamentary session, the government has moved to withdraw the Delimitation Bill, 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha in April. The Centre has replaced it with a revised version that provides for a 50 per cent increase in the number of seats in Parliament and state and Union Territory assemblies, while seeking to give effect to women's reservation.The reasons for withdrawing the original legislation were outlined in a statement signed by minister of state for law and justice (independent charge) Arjun Ram Meghwal on November 27.The proposed replacement, titled the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, makes substantial changes to the original legislation, particularly regarding the constitution of the Delimitation Commission, the use of Census figures, the allocation of seats reserved for women and the expansion of legislative representation.The original Delimitation Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16, 2026, along with the Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-first Amendment) Bill, 2026, and the Union Territories Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026.The three Bills were brought in to facilitate the setting up of a Delimitation Commission to readjust the allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and state and Union Territory Assemblies and redraw constituency boundaries.However, the Constitution Amendment Bill failed to secure the special majority required under Article 368 of the Constitution when it was put to consideration on April 17. Consequently, the two related Bills were not taken up further and the original Delimitation Bill remained pending in the Lok Sabha.What changes in the revised BillThe revised legislation expands the scope of delimitation to include provisions for implementing women's reservation in the Lok Sabha and state and Union Territory assemblies.It also requires the Centre to constitute the Delimitation Commission as soon as possible after the proposed legislation comes into force, instead of setting it up "from time to time", as provided in the original Bill.Another significant change is the use of "latest census figures", defined as the most recent Census figures published on the date the proposed legislation comes into force. This means the 2011 Census would be used if no newer Census figures are published before the legislation takes effect. The Commission will use these figures to readjust seat allocation and redraw territorial constituencies.50 per cent uniform increase in seatsThe revised legislation also provides that seats reserved for women will be allotted through rotation in a manner decided by the Delimitation Commission. It further proposes a 50 per cent increase in the number of seats allocated to each state and Union Territory in the Lok Sabha and the total number of seats in their respective legislative assemblies during the first delimitation exercise after the proposed Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-second Amendment) Act, 2026, comes into force.The Bill adds that the quota would run for 15 years from the commencement of the 2023 amendment, with Parliament empowered to extend it by law, according to news agency PTI.The government has said the uniform increase would enhance overall representation while maintaining the existing relative distribution of seats among states.The government has proposed withdrawing the original Bill under clause (b) of Rule 110 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Lok Sabha, as the revised legislation substantially alters its provisions.27-Nov-delimitationGet the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Passenger denied alcohol on birthday flight over exit-row rule sparks online debate
articles.summary: A traveler claims a flight attendant refused to serve him alcohol in the exit row on a birthday flight to Puerto Rico. Federal regulations do not ban alcohol in exit rows.
articles.body: For one traveler heading to San Juan recently to celebrate his birthday, the extra legroom of an exit row came with an unexpected catch: a no-alcohol flight. Boarding a four-hour Saturday evening flight before his birthday, the passenger was informed by a flight attendant that alcohol would not be served to anyone seated in an exit row, according to the individual's viral post on Reddit. The sudden restriction caught the flyer — who said he hadn't had a single drink all day — off guard. AMERICANS EYEING DREAM VACATION TRIP WARNED THAT RESCUE CREWS COULD TAKE DAYS TO REACH THEM While federal regulations require exit-row passengers to be alert and capable of assisting in an emergency, there is no blanket ban on serving them a drink, according to FAA regulations. "Being called to assist in an emergency in an exit row is about a one in a million occurrence," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and blog author of "View From The Wing," told Fox News Digital. "There are multiple passengers in the exit row, and a single drink is not likely to impair your ability to assist in that situation," he said. Leff said it's not clear from the account whether the flight attendant knew about FAA and airline guidance regarding alcohol in exit rows. (Leff was not on the flight in question nor was he connected to it.) UNRULY PASSENGERS COULD BE BANNED FOR LIFE FROM MULTIPLE AIRLINES UNDER NEW PROPOSAL "Sometimes, crew members get things wrong," said Leff. He said in such a case, "the best thing to do is to talk to someone else on board, but certainly not to escalate things." He added, "Making up a policy may have the opposite effect because somebody may know that's wrong, and they may be … righteously outraged over it." VIRAL PLANE-ETIQUETTE DEBATE ERUPTS AFTER MAN GRABS PASSENGER’S AISLE SEAT TO SIT WITH WIFE Online, Reddit users emphasized they saw the flight attendant's actions as a huge gaffe. One summed it up this way: "That’s definitely [an] FA policy, not FAA." "That’s not a policy," one commenter said. "Sounds like you ran into a tyrant that makes up whatever rules they want on the spot," the person added, directly addressing the original poster. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Another person said he had flown one airline about 70 times in the past year and almost always sat in the exit row, adding, "Almost always get a drink. Definitely not a regulation." Someone else commented, "I sat in the exit row on my birthday five days ago. The [flight attendant] made a point to tell me drinks were on them because it was my birthday. I had a tequila soda. No issues." Others, however, supported the flight attendant's move, arguing that exit-row passengers may need to help during an emergency. "Seems like a good policy," one person said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Another person said he or she would like the assurance that "the person opening the emergency exit isn’t sloshed." ‘Morally outraged’ The Reddit poster who was denied the birthday drink wrote that the airline issued a standard "sorry for how this was communicated" apology alongside 5,000 frequent flyer miles. "Almost always get a drink. Definitely not a regulation." "If a passenger in this case is getting 5,000 mileage plus miles, those are worth [around] $50.75 dollars, certainly more than the single drink was worth," Leff said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The passenger may feel morally outraged for having had the wrong information … especially in that moment," he added. "But they can now go buy several [drinks] with the relative economic value they've received in exchange." Leff explained, however, that flight attendants are not allowed to serve alcohol to passengers who have already had a number of drinks. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Airlines are not supposed to serve alcohol to passengers who are … already visibly intoxicated. There are limits to that service," he said. "Passengers are also not supposed to access their own alcohol … precisely because crew members are supposed to monitor," said Leff. "And they don't want these things getting out of hand."
